detail:
NIAMS states the goals of Raynaud's treatment plainly: reduce how many attacks happen, make attacks less severe, prevent tissue damage, and prevent loss of finger or toe tissue. Because primary Raynaud's phenomenon does not lead to tissue damage, nondrug treatment is used first: dressing warmly, warming hands and feet during an attack, and avoiding triggers such as cold exposure and, where relevant, smoking.

Treatment with medicine is more common in secondary Raynaud's phenomenon. NIAMS describes blood pressure medicines that relax blood vessels among the options, and a kind that can be applied to the fingers to heal ulcers. Severe cases can lead to sores or gangrene in the fingers and toes, which is why new ulcers or non-healing skin changes need prompt care.

Talk to your doctor before starting or changing any medication.

sourceVideoTitle: Raynaud's Phenomenon: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take (NIAMS)
summary: NIAMS guidance aims treatment at fewer and less severe attacks and at preventing tissue damage: nondrug measures come first for primary Raynaud's, while medicines that relax blood vessels are used more often for the secondary form.
takeaways: keep the whole body warm, not just the hands
warm hands promptly when an attack starts
calcium channel blockers are a common prescription option
ulcers or blackened skin need prompt medical care
title: Managing Raynaud's: warmth first, medicines when needed
